excerpt: He was seventeen when he went to war and knew the street talk of Los Angeles. In the dark jungles of Saipan, Guy Gabaldon walked alone into enemy lines and brought back fifteen hundred men without firing a shot. A sharp, unsparing account of courage, the quiet horror of the cliffs, and a Marine who did his job and went home
author: Lexi Zotomayor
bodyText:
Who would have thought that learning Japanese as a boy growing up in East Los Angeles would prove to be the essential asset in Guy Gabaldon’s back pocket when he landed on Saipan in 1944? Life has a curious way of preparing us for things we cannot possibly anticipate, arranging small, scattered pieces of an early life until they suddenly fit together under the violent pressures of history.

Guy was seventeen when he enlisted in the Marines. He was small, sharp-witted, and spoke the casual, daily Japanese of his neighborhood friends. On Saipan, that language—spoken not from a military handbook, but with the familiar cadence of home—became a bridge across an abyss. Walking into the dark jungles and dark caves alone, he talked more than fifteen hundred Japanese soldiers and terrified civilians into stepping out into the light. They called him the Pied Piper of Saipan.

He saw the worst of the war—the women holding their children and jumping from the high, sheer cliffs of Marpi because they had believed the propaganda of fear. He saved many, but the ones he couldn't save stayed with him. War does something strange to a man’s internal geography; it fastens him forever to the ground where he saw life and death stripped down to their rawest elements. For Gabaldon, that ground was Saipan. Though Hollywood later tried to frame his life in dramatic celluloid and newsprint, he didn't care much for big talk. He simply came back. He brought his family, made a life on the island, and stayed for two decades, living quietly under the shadow of Mount Tapochau.

I was working at the *Marianas Variety* in late August of 2006 when word came that Gabaldon had passed away in Florida at the age of eighty. Not long after, his remains were flown back home to Saipan, where he was given a hero’s welcome.

In a newsroom, you see history arrive in fragments—press releases, official statements, flight schedules, and black-and-white photographs. But when you stand in the presence of a family, history softens into something deeply personal. I remember meeting his wife and his son, Josh. Standing near them, you could feel the quiet weight of a long journey coming to an end. They had brought him back to the place that had defined his youth, haunted his middle years, and ultimately held his heart.

They took his ashes up to the highest point of the island, on Mount Tapochau, and scattered them into the trade winds. Looking up at the peak, it seemed entirely fitting. The boy from East L.A. had finally come to rest in the soil of the island he had spent a lifetime trying to heal.

title: Saipan's Pied Piper
